intro: The 2026 midterms sent shockwaves through the AI industry this week, as voters across the country passed measures restricting data center construction and Texas — now home to Elon Musk's corporate empire — turned blue, proving that backlash against Big Tech's physical footprint has become a genuinely bipartisan force. Meanwhile, the global tug-of-war over AI's boundaries continues on multiple fronts, from Australia's copyright fight with the music industry to troubling new details about alleged Chinese espionage targeting Nvidia's CEO and a shell company quietly buying advanced American chips. It's a day that reminds us the biggest AI stories aren't always about the models themselves — they're about the power struggles surrounding them.

stories.title: Global music body warns Australia against weakening AI copyright law
stories.summary: The IFPI has warned Australian PM Albanese that loosening copyright protections to give AI companies broad access to online content would be a 'disaster for creativity,' as Australia faces pressure from big tech seeking looser rules for AI training.
stories.opinion: The music industry's most powerful international body is drawing a clear line against Australia caving to tech lobby pressure on AI training data rights.

stories.title: Google's Gemini product head shares lessons on building frontier AI models
stories.summary: Tulsee Doshi, Head of Product for Google's Gemini and other frontier AI models, discusses her 60-20-20 framework for balancing investment, argues model development resembles 'potion-making' more than pure engineering, and says both formal evals and subjective 'vibes' matter for assessing model quality.
stories.opinion: An unusually candid look inside Google's AI product development revealing how much art and intuition still drives what is marketed as cutting-edge engineering.

stories.title: Midterm results deal blow to data centers and Elon Musk's political spending
stories.summary: The 2026 U.S. midterm elections delivered a historic Democratic victory, with voters across the country passing ballot measures restricting data center construction. Texas elected governor Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned on restricting data centers, defeating incumbent Greg Abbott. Elon Musk donated over half a billion dollars to Republicans with little return, and his companies are now headquartered in a state that turned blue. Data center opposition has become a bipartisan grassroots issue.
stories.opinion: Data center opposition has calcified into a genuine grassroots political movement, and Musk's massive political spending looks like one of the worst return-on-investment stories in recent political history.

stories.title: NYT Cooking's AI assistant helps with weeknight meals but stumbles on baking
stories.summary: The Verge tested NYT Cooking's new AI assistant on iOS, finding it useful for ingredient swaps and recipe improvisation in everyday cooking but nearly disastrous for baking, where precision matters more. AI cooking tools are proliferating through Alexa Plus, Samsung Food, and cooking robots.
stories.opinion: A useful illustration of where AI assistants excel — flexible, forgiving tasks — versus where they fail — precision-dependent work like baking.

stories.title: Tom Gauld cartoon comments on AI prompts and writing
stories.summary: The Guardian published a Tom Gauld cartoon on November 8, 2026, about prompts for a cartoon about artificial intelligence and writing. The cartoon itself is only viewable on the Guardian's website.
stories.opinion: A meta-commentary on AI's relationship to creative work from one of the Guardian's most distinctive cartoonists.

stories.title: More details emerge on China's alleged recruitment of exec to spy on Nvidia CEO
stories.summary: A U.S. intelligence memo claims Alice Huang of Singapore-based Megaspeed was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The Financial Times reported the memo alleges a romantic relationship between the two. Nvidia said Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were 'not unusual' and the company does not share classified information with customers. Separately, the NYT found that New Matrix, a Chinese company authorized to buy Nvidia chips, appears to be a shell with ties to a blacklisted Chinese private equity firm.
stories.opinion: The story is deepening with increasingly uncomfortable details for Nvidia, and the parallel New Matrix revelations suggest systemic failures in chip export controls. Where coverage differs: The Verge (yesterday) describes the relationship between the two Huangs as 'close'; TechCrunch (citing Financial Times) reports the memo alleges a 'romantic relationship'

stories.title: US allowed Nvidia to sell advanced AI chips to apparent Chinese shell company
stories.summary: The New York Times reports that New Matrix, a firm approved to buy Nvidia's H200 AI chips, appears to be a shell company with empty offices, no online presence, and ties to a Chinese private equity firm blacklisted by the US government since 2024. The sales became possible after the Trump administration relaxed Biden-era chip restrictions following Nvidia's agreement to give the government a 15 percent cut of all sales, alongside intense lobbying by CEO Jensen Huang.
stories.opinion: A damning indictment of how Nvidia's lobbying and the Trump administration's relaxed export controls may have enabled exactly the technology transfer the restrictions were designed to prevent.

stories.title: The case against relentless optimization: why efficiency makes systems fragile
stories.summary: Using examples from hospital bed occupancy to financial markets and transportation, the article argues that running systems at maximum capacity leaves no buffer for crises. Slack, redundancy, and apparent 'waste' are essential for resilience, and our obsession with eliminating inefficiency creates systemic vulnerabilities.
stories.opinion: A timely philosophical counterpoint to the Silicon Valley efficiency gospel, particularly relevant as AI promises to optimize everything further.

stories.title: Former Meta security chief says AI has broken cybersecurity
stories.summary: Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and Stanford lecturer, argues on The Verge's Decoder podcast that AI-boosted attacks have created a 'dark age' in cybersecurity. He says the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry is failing against AI-enhanced attacks from private and state actors like Russia and North Korea, though he believes this is a difficult transitional period rather than a permanent state.
stories.opinion: A sobering assessment from a highly credible voice that the cybersecurity industry's current tools and approaches are fundamentally inadequate for the AI era.

tweet_headlines.author: itspdfu
tweet_headlines.headline: macOS 27.3 tightens Full Disk Access: __automatic denials are no longer saved to TCC__, so users must manually add apps using the + button.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
macOS 27.3 starts implementing changes to Full Disk Access (FDA). Here’s what ‘very explicit user action’ may mean.

When an app tries to read a protected file without FDA, macOS doesn’t prompt the user to grant permission. Instead, it automatically denies access and records that denial in the TCC database.

Once in the db, apps show up under Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access with their toggle off. Apps will often add themselves to the list, then instruct the user to open Settings and flip the toggle.

Not anymore: starting with macOS 27.3 and feature flag TCC/FDA_WARNING, automatic denials are no longer saved. Users will have to explicitly add an app to the list with the + button or by dragging it in from Applications.

So far, the flag doesn’t add any additional warnings or dialogs, but its name suggests these may arrive in future betas. The flag is disabled in 27.3 beta 1.

——

Relatedly, macOS 27.3 introduces “Private Folders,” a new folder-by-folder permission configured like Full Disk Access. Not fully wired up yet, but it could offer a narrower alternative to Full Disk Access.

It’s also impacted by TCC/FDA_WARNING: when the flag is on, automatic Private Folders denials aren’t saved either.

tweet_headlines.author: TomSolidPM
tweet_headlines.headline: Tom Solid found Grok Bot __burns through its weekly allowance faster than Claude Code__ and needed constant nudging to keep a five-bot team on task across 24 hours.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
I cannot trust Grok Bot with important work.

I've run several tests comparing it with Claude Code.

I've already praised its speed, responsiveness, accessibility and ease of use.

But two problems are killing it for me:
usage consumption and reliability.

On Ultra, I'm burning through my weekly allowance faster than I ever have with Claude, even back when I was using Fable 5.1. And I can't rely on it to finish the job.

For this test, I had five dedicated Grok Bots working as a team for over 24h. I constantly had to nudge them to keep going. A lot of their updates and conversations with each other were nonsense.

After 24h, I stopped the work and asked for a comprehensive handoff covering everything they'd done, including all files and code produced.

Then I had Claude Code run an audit using an agent swarm. Part of the report is what you're seeing in the image.

They'd produced A LOT of code. 9,300 lines.

And as the highlighted finding shows, none of that code wasn't even needed in the first place.

This test burned through 40% of my weekly allowance on a $200/month plan. Are you kidding me?

Claude Code is fixing it now. Based on my previous tests, I expect it to consume far less of my allowance.

I'm back to manually orchestrating my agents for anything beyond simple research or lookups.

If that's all I can trust Grok Bot with, is it really worth keeping the subscription?

tweet_headlines.author: ducksays
tweet_headlines.headline: ducksays hit __1.33M impressions in two weeks__ using a Grok companion bot named "HoMI" that scouts and filters research so they're not the ideas bottleneck.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
i got 1.33M impressions over the last 2 weeks, with help from my grok @bot.

here's how its scout finds and filters research in 7 steps:

my CMO has a companion bot named "HoMI" (head of market intelligence). i'm building this so i'm not the bottleneck for ideas.

1. find the builders

look for smaller accounts repeatedly sharing useful grok bot setups, results and how-tos. not just one viral post.

2. organize the sources

keep watch lists for builders, news and peers. let HoMI maintain a list on your x account and treat it like its following.

3. spot unusual performance

flag posts getting roughly 3x that creator's usual views or bookmarks. compare similar-age posts where possible

4. check the substance

big numbers aren't always enough. useful workflows, verified updates and real failures can matter without going viral.

5. capture the evidence

bring back the source, the numbers and why it might matter. mark anything unverified.

6. hand it to my CMO

my CMO checks the findings against my actual work and pitches worthwhile angles before drafting. a finding isn't automatically a post.

7. clean the lists

drop spam and off-topic accounts so the research stays relevant.

HoMI finds the evidence. my CMO shapes the pitches.

i still bring the firsthand experience, choose what's worth sharing and hit publish.

tweet_headlines.author: YoussefHosni951
tweet_headlines.headline: Youssef Hosni argues your CLAUDE.md is bloated — Claude Code supports __path-specific rules that load only for matching files__.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Your CLAUDE.md might be making Claude Code less effective. You don't need to load every coding rule into every session.

Many developers keep adding or asking the agent to add instructions to CLAUDE.md whenever Claude makes a mistake.

Eventually, the file contains rules about backend APIs, React components, database migrations, tests, documentation, and deployment.

But if Claude is fixing a frontend component, why should it need all the database migration instructions?

Claude Code supports path-specific rules that load when it works with matching files.

For example, create .claude/rules/api.md:

---
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts
---
# API Rules
- Validate all incoming requests.
- Use the standard error format.
- Add tests for new endpoints

Claude Code loads this rule when its file tools access matching API files. When it works only with unrelated files, the rule isn't loaded.

You can create separate files for frontend, testing, and database conventions.

This reduces unnecessary instructions in the active context and makes the rules easier to maintain.

It is particularly useful for large repositories where different directories follow different conventions. It is still guidance rather than a hard enforcement mechanism.

tweet_headlines.author: KacperRutk
tweet_headlines.headline: GrokBot's docs lay out a clean multi-agent design rule: __give a job its own bot__ once it has recurring sources, its own schedule, or specific rules.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
I feel like the main question I get regarding @bot is when do I create another bot? How do I know?

Well, let's take a look at the docs together.

GrokBot's docs give you a useful rule for when to create another bot.

Start new work with your primary bot. It's your main point of contact and can pass work to your other bots.

When the same request keeps coming back with its own sources, rules or schedule, give that job its own bot.

That bot builds up memory for the job, including the preferences and instructions you give it.

For example, a weekly research report might deserve its own bot once you know which sources to use and what the report should include.

But separate bots aren't separate computers.

They share the cloud computer, its files and browser sign-ins. Each has its own screen and memory, with some basic facts about you shared across bots.

So give bots clear responsibilities, but don't treat a new bot as a private place to keep sensitive files.

Try asking your primary bot:

"Look at the work I keep bringing you. Which recurring job would benefit from its own bot? Explain what that bot would do and what you would still handle."

If you have not taken a look at the upgraded GrokBot doc's you absolutely should. Shout @mattyp and the @spacexai team for their attention to detail.
